item.title: Decomposition Atlases of Brains and Kidneys from Postmortem CT: Shape and Topological Data Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.00278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forensic assessments of postmortem decomposition often rely on external, whole-body signs, yet structural changes within organs remain largely unquantified. Using whole-body computed tomography scans of 59 decedents from the New Mexico Decedent Image Database, we conduct an organ-level statistical shape analysis of decomposing brains and kidneys, representing each organ as a three-dimensional point cloud of its outer surface and internal cavity boundaries. Decomposition creates voids, fragmentation, and structural heterogeneity, complicating point correspondence. Registration-based principal component analysis and principal nested cones yield interpretable orderings for brains only. We therefore construct a registration-free pipeline using persistent homology and a fusion of complementary topological distances selected through simulations of cavity formation and growth. Clustering identifies broad patterns of internal decay, and seriation produces organ-specific decomposition atlases. The brain atlas combines geometric and topological rankings; the kidney atlas uses topology alone. Rank agreement is higher between paired kidneys (Kendall's $\tau = 0.59$) than between brains and kidneys ($\tau = 0.34$ to $0.39$), indicating asynchronous decompositions within a body. Whole-body stages agree more closely with brain than with kidney rankings. These findings support quantitative forensic taphonomy by complementing whole-body staging with organ-level, interior-based measurements. We release the organ point clouds and analysis code to support research on organ decomposition and shape analysis without reliable correspondence.
item.dc:creator: Yanyan Zhan, Yuexuan Wu, Ian L. Dryden, Zeloso M. Tiago, Edward C. Schwalbe

item.title: Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceutical Development: Building Rigorous, Decision-Ready Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2611.00557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are reshaping the pharmaceutical lifecycle, from discovery and clinical development through manufacturing and regulatory review to safety surveillance and health economics, creating evidentiary challenges that predictive performance alone cannot address. This review examines the inferential, causal, validation, and documentation requirements for AI-enabled evidence generation in high-stakes settings and argues that they must be built into workflows. We outline the evidentiary functions that AI-derived outputs must satisfy before supporting consequential decisions: estimand definition, fit-for-purpose data collection, bias control, uncertainty quantification, validation, interpretability, and decision-grade documentation. Because AI both depends on and accelerates large-scale, non-randomized data collection, the integration of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with real-world data (RWD) is where its evidentiary risks concentrate; we therefore present a five-step causal roadmap for that integration, in which external data supplement but never replace a concurrent control, and characterize the safeguards required across development, pharmacovigilance, regulation, and health technology assessment. Priority frontiers answer recurring implementation problems: conformal prediction for overconfident predictions, randomization-based inference for scarce data, and federated causal inference and privacy-preserving generative modeling for data that cannot be pooled. Evidence generation depends not on competition between RCTs and RWD, or between statistics and AI/ML, but on their principled synthesis under causal and inferential frameworks, with statistical expertise central to decision-ready evidence.
item.dc:creator: Xin Luo, Margaret Gamalo, Achilleas Livieratos, Maria Kudela, Qilu Yu, Yunxun Wang, Junjing Lin, Yuxi Zhao, Allshine Chen

item.title: Certified computation of Buehler confidence limits for system reliability
item.description: arXiv:2611.00711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Component tests can support a lower confidence limit for a system that has not been tested as a whole, but numerical optimization can compromise its coverage. A feasible point in the minimization defining a Buehler limit gives an upper bound on that limit; reporting it can therefore overstate reliability. We develop a computation that maintains lower and upper bounds on the ideal endpoint for a prescribed ordering. Bounds over entire parameter regions justify the reported lower endpoint at every completed checkpoint, including under adaptive stopping and selection among runs. Separate refinement conditions establish convergence, and an explicit error allocation accounts for simulated tail probabilities and confidence-region localization. The theory retains nuisance and dependence parameters in the observation model. Monotone corner bounds give the implemented specialization for scalar and two-component binomial systems; Bernstein and probability-distance bounds provide further theoretical constructions. Four benchmark problems reach a certified width of $10^{-5}$ under each of four search strategies. Additional stochastic candidates increase cost without reducing subdivisions, whereas complete sample-space enumeration verifies the implemented coverage at three parameter vectors. For the all-success example, the certified lower limit is $0.68128$, compared with $0.41738$ from Bonferroni-adjusted component limits.
item.dc:creator: Zhaohui Li

item.title: Power-optimal allocation in multi-arm cluster randomized trials
item.description: arXiv:2611.00842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper discusses a power-based framework for optimal allocation in multi-arm cluster randomized trials with continuous or binary outcomes, allowing cluster sizes and within-cluster correlations to differ across treatment groups. We consider optimal cluster allocation with prespecified cluster sizes as well as joint optimization of cluster allocations and sizes. Using generalized estimating equations to account for correlated outcomes and a quasi-score test to assess treatment homogeneity, we derive locally optimal designs, which depend on specified parameter values. Since locally optimal designs can be highly sensitive to changes in the parameter values, we also propose maximin designs, which maximize the minimum power over a prescribed parameter space and provide robust allocations under parameter uncertainty. We analytically characterize the maximin designs and the least favorable configurations of treatment means and provide procedures for determining the sample size required to attain a target power. Applications to the WASH Benefits Bangladesh and SCORE trials illustrate gains in calculated power and reductions in the required sample size relative to the original trial designs.
item.dc:creator: Muneeb Ahmad Wani, Satya Prakash Singh

item.title: Searching for related contributors to a DNA mixture using single cell analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.01782v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a staged process for assessing the presence of related individuals in an autosomal STR DNA mixture sample, when it is analysed using a single cell pipeline analysis (as opposed to a bulk mixture analysis). In the absence of a large dataset if single cells from real related people, artificial single cell data is generated by sampling individual locus data taken from single cell dataset of real unrelated people. It is applied to create random admixtures used in a relatedness search for pairs of individuals to illustrate the usefulness of the method.
item.dc:creator: Robert Cowell

item.title: Empirical rather than simulated spectral band adjustment of MODIS to Sentinel-3 OLCI for European vegetation monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2611.02212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectral band adjustment derived from convolved spectra describes sensor differences under controlled conditions, but its applicability to operational products requires assessment. We compare this approach with adjustment estimated directly from MODIS and Sentinel-3 OLCI observations for European vegetation monitoring. Both streams undergo atmospheric correction and Ross-Thick/Li-Sparse Reciprocal BRDF normalization to nadir viewing and local solar noon. Using observations from 2019-2024, we derive annual OLCI/MODIS reflectance-ratio relationships with unadjusted MODIS NDVI. The operational correction uses quadratic red and linear near-infrared (NIR) functions. We compare these relationships with irradiance-weighted canopy simulations and assess the empirical correction at 460 locations. Simulated and empirical relationships differ, particularly for red reflectance at high NDVI. Background-dependent simulated ratios also demonstrate the limitations of a single NDVI-based function. The empirical correction reduces red and NIR root-mean-square error (RMSE) at 66.3% and 71.1% of locations, with median paired reductions of 5.98% and 13.67%. Median paired RMSE decreases by 0.86% for NDVI but increases by 0.95% for EVI2, 0.74% for NIRv and 7.07% for the Plant Phenology Index (PPI), calculated with stream-specific historical references. This study establishes an operational empirical adjustment and shows that the specified spectral simulation does not reproduce the relationship between the normalized products. It provides evidence for improved reflectance consistency while demonstrating that vegetation-index benefits require separate assessment.
item.dc:creator: Hongxiao Jin

item.title: Leveraging Continuous Trade Data for Intraday Imbalance Price Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2611.03331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forecasts of imbalance prices are essential for participants in short-term electricity markets. This study proposes an approach to integrate trade data from continuous intraday markets into forecasting methods and considers the production of both parametric and non-parametric density forecasts. Extensive feature engineering is required to convert irregular trade data into a suitable tabular structure. Our findings demonstrate that intraday trade data can enhance state-of-the-art forecasts based on quantile regression and LASSO. We also propose a model based on Natural Gradient Boosting to predict the means and variances of a bimodal Gaussian mixture, which offers both improved predictive performance and computational efficiency. In a case study based on multiple years of data from Great Britain, our proposed approach reduced the Pinball Loss of state-of-the-art models by 20% for forecasts made 30 seconds before gate closure, and by 7.5% for forecasts made one hour before delivery.
item.dc:creator: Klimis Stylpnopoulos, Jethro Browell, Janine Illian, Ciaran Gilbert, Wayne Jones

item.title: Transformer-Based Reinforcement Learning for Phase I Dose Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2611.00395v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Phase I dose-finding trials must learn from sparse toxicity observations while limiting exposure to overly toxic doses. We develop a single reinforcement-learning policy for trials with different numbers of ordered dose levels. Each dose is represented as a token containing its normalized position, accumulated patient count, observed dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs), and current-dose indicator. A Transformer encoder summarizes the dose tokens, trial-conditioned cross-attention produces a fixed-dimensional trial representation, and a three-action policy chooses de-escalation, staying, or escalation. The final maximum tolerated dose (MTD) decision is deliberately kept outside the learned policy: after the planned sample size, weighted isotonic regression and a prespecified safety cap select the dose closest to the target toxicity probability. In the simulations, toxicity-penalized policies reduce DLT burden while unpenalized policies improve selection accuracy at the cost of greater toxicity. These results demonstrate a controllable safety--accuracy trade-off but do not establish superiority over conventional dose-finding designs.
item.dc:creator: Shijie Yuan

item.title: Characterizing Estimator-Regime Transitions in Adaptive Enrichment Trials
item.description: arXiv:2611.00549v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Adaptive enrichment trials that identify responsive subpopulations allocate a fixed sample across them and estimate each one's effect from the resulting data. For a synthetic control design with adaptive recruitment and borrowing of control outcomes, we ask whether a doubly robust family of targeted maximum likelihood estimators should replace its sample mean; the choice can be made largely at the design stage. A crossing condition weighs the bias removed and the efficiency gained by the doubly robust family against the finite-sample inflation of nuisance estimation; an equal-error boundary, located by simulation, separates the families in the plane of sample size and bias. A consistency principle prices recruiting with the wrong family's variance functional. With three and eight simulated subpopulations the boundary's sign prediction for the mean squared error difference holds in $99.6\%$ of $10{,}302$ comparisons decided at two standard errors. A pre-specified selector commits to the doubly robust family where the squared anticipated bias exceeds the net variance term. Recruiting along that family's path costs up to $0.035$ in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; recruiting with the sample mean functional and routing only the analysis removes this cost and about nine tenths of its error excess.
item.dc:creator: Xin Luo, Maria Kudela, Margaret Gamalo

item.title: A Bayesian Magnitude-Composition Model for Tree-Size Distributions and Stand-Tables
item.description: arXiv:2611.00938v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sparse forest inventories often provide too few plots to estimate species-specific tree-size distributions for individual stands. We develop a general Bayesian magnitude-composition model that separates overall abundance from its allocation among categories. A negative-binomial model describes total counts, while multinomial models describe how those counts are allocated among categories. In forest inventory, this construction allocates trees among species and then size classes within species, without imposing a parametric form on the tree-size distribution. Covariates inform both abundance and composition. Shared latent factors represent residual spatial and group-level dependence among categories using relatively few processes, while smoothing priors on regression coefficients borrow information across neighboring size classes. Nearest-neighbor Gaussian processes support efficient spatial computation. Joint posterior prediction and area-weighted aggregation yield stand-tables---tree densities by species and size class---and derived measures such as size-class diversity, with associated uncertainty. Simulations show small estimation errors and near-nominal predictive-interval coverage for forest and stand summaries. An application combining field plots and light detection and ranging (LiDAR) covariates illustrates estimation of species-specific distributions of diameter at breast height and size-class diversity in sampled and unsampled stands.
item.dc:creator: Andrew O. Finley, Malcolm S. Itter, Arthur Spitta, Arne Nothdurft

item.title: A model-based adaptive sampling framework for infectious disease surveillance
item.description: arXiv:2611.01199v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Longitudinal surveillance must choose each round's sampling design before the next observations arrive. Fixed sample-size rules treat each round as an isolated cross-sectional survey and ignore the evolving uncertainty in the epidemic process, which changes as transmission, vaccination, interventions, variants, and behavior change. We present a model-based adaptive sampling framework for choosing the next-round design. A state-space model represents the epidemic process and maps latent states to surveillance estimands. A statistical filter calibrates the model as observations arrive, propagating uncertainty in latent states, time-varying parameters, stochastic dynamics, and sampling noise. A Bayesian assurance criterion converts the one-step-ahead predictive distribution into the minimum-cost design likely to achieve a target posterior credible-interval width. We evaluated the framework in two simulations and in a retrospective case study of SARS-CoV-2 serosurveillance among Canadian blood donors in four regions, replaying the series with each week's specimens subsampled to the selected design. In simulations, the policy increased sampling effort during an anticipated high-variance period, and the share of intervals meeting the width target (0.970) agreed with validated assurance (0.974). After an unanticipated change in transmission rate, validated assurance stayed at 0.960 while the share meeting the target fell to 0.894 (95% Monte Carlo interval 0.869 to 0.919) in the transition window. Sampling effort rose while the filter relearned the transmission rate, then fell. In the case study, recommended sample sizes tracked the one-step predictive uncertainty and were largest during the Omicron wave, and the 90% filtering interval had width at most 0.10 in 94% of region-rounds with specimens. The modular framework extends to other pathogens, data streams, and surveillance objectives.
item.dc:creator: Supun Manathunga, Nathaniel Osgood, Sheila F. O'Brien, David L. Buckeridge, W. Alton Russell

item.title: Accuracy Is Not Risk: Why Medical AI Should Not Report Only Its Most Likely Label
item.description: arXiv:2611.01312v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Background. Many medical AI models are trained to reproduce a single reference label and hand the most likely label to the next step in a clinical workflow. A classifier can select that label correctly while providing an inadequate summary for estimating downstream risk. Methods. We use Jeffrey's rule of conditioning to specify when probabilities over intermediate states, such as diagnoses or imaging categories, can be carried forward to an outcome risk. We separate two errors of reporting only the most likely label, discarding the probability of the other states and applying the risk of patients who have the leading diagnosis to a patient who only probably has it. We also give conditions under which the label and the full distribution lead to the same decision, and we propose guardrails for device developers, regulatory reviewers, and health insurers. Results. In a hypothetical chest-pain differential, reporting only the benign leading diagnosis greatly understates the patient's risk of death or cardiac arrest, so a patient who warrants evaluation could be discharged or denied imaging. In a hypothetical BI-RADS example, the most likely category is "probably benign," yet the propagated malignancy risk exceeds the ceiling that defines that category. Conclusions. A predicted label is not an observed state, and a calibrated classifier is not automatically a valid outcome model. Clinical and insurance coverage decisions should rest on the patient's outcome risk, judged against a threshold justified by the consequences of acting and not acting. Developers should state what each model output means and check that every step between the model and the decision preserves the patient's risk.
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Humpherys, Makoto Jones

item.title: Sentiment sensing: comparative analysis of multilingual sentiment dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.01348v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cross-country sentiment analysis faces three fundamental challenges: language-specific biases distort comparisons, compositional data constraints invalidate standard statistics and temporal dynamics lack rigorous testing frameworks. We introduce sentiment sensing, a framework that addresses these gaps through integrated statistical methods. By combining compositional data analysis, functional data methods, and non-parametric inference, sentiment sensing enables valid multilingual comparisons and statistically defensible detection of sentiment shifts. Our framework has been tested in two case studies, analyzing news articles from the 27 countries of the European Union on the topics of energy and artificial intelligence. Sentiment sensing focuses on multilingual sentiment analysis enabling rigorous comparative science.
item.dc:creator: Mara Sabina Bernardi, Elisa Di Nuovo, Francesca Torti, Giuseppe Tirone, Nicolas Stefanovitch, Zsuzsanna Pasztor, Charles Macmillan, Domenico Perrotta, Bertrand De Longueville

item.title: The precision of fractional factorial designs under randomization
item.description: arXiv:2611.01949v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A regular fraction of a two-level factorial design runs fewer treatment combinations (cells), with more units in each. With the number of units fixed, more units per cell do not by themselves reduce the variance. Averaged over the fractions of one defining contrast subgroup, a fraction's variance is smaller than the full design's by the unit-to-unit variation of the aliased effects, a gain the usual variance estimator misses. Assuming the aliased effects are zero, we propose a full-design estimator that weights the fractions' contrasts by inverse variance. Its estimated variance never exceeds the saturated estimator's. In large samples, it is proportional to the harmonic mean of the fractions' average cell variances, and a fraction's, on average, to the arithmetic mean. We test this assumption, but choosing between the two estimators by the test can lose coverage. The results extend to unequal allocations, and the large-sample results to covariate adjustment.
item.dc:creator: Xinyuan Chen

item.title: A multivariate unsupervised lognormal-GPD mixture for dependent losses
item.description: arXiv:2611.02148v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a multivariate two-population mixture distribution for heavy-tailed and positively skewed non-negative data. The first mixture population is a multivariate lognormal, while the second is a distribution obtained by joining univariate zero-mean generalized Pareto densities via a Gumbel copula. The model is unsupervised, since no threshold has to be set or estimated. We derive some properties of the distribution and develop an Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm for maximum likelihood estimation, which is found to perform well in multivariate contexts beyond the bivariate case. The finite-sample properties of the estimators are assessed by means of simulation experiments, and an empirical application to aggregated commercial property-casualty insurance claims illustrates the impact of dependence on risk estimation. All the methods are implemented in the R package MultLognGPD, available on Github.
item.dc:creator: Marco Bee, Flavio Santi

item.title: One-Sample Mendelian Randomization and Instrumental Variable Analyses in R and Stata: The OneSampleMR and ivonesamplemr Packages
item.description: arXiv:2611.02887v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants as instrumental variables (IVs) to estimate the causal effect of an exposure on an outcome. When individual-level data on the instruments, exposure, and outcome are available in a single sample (one-sample MR), a range of IV estimators can be used beyond the standard two-stage least squares estimator, including structural mean models (SMMs) and two-stage predictor substitu- tion (TSPS) and two-stage residual inclusion (TSRI) estimators with nonlinear second stage models. These estimators are important when the outcome is binary, where in- vestigators typically wish to report causal risk ratios or causal odds ratios. However, implementations of these estimators are scattered across software packages and are of- ten unavailable with standard errors that account for the estimation of the first stage. We describe two packages which implement these estimators: OneSampleMR for R and ivonesamplemr for Stata. Both packages fit the multiplicative and logistic SMMs and TSPS and TSRI estimators with identity, log-additive, log-multiplicative, and logit links using the generalized method of moments (GMM), so that the standard errors account for the uncertainty in both stages of estimation. OneSampleMR additionally provides the Sanderson-Windmeijer conditional F-statistic for assessing instrument strength in models with multiple exposures, and ivonesamplemr additionally provides prefix commands for moving window and within-quantile estimation for exploring nonlinear exposure-outcome relationships. We illustrate both packages using the same simulated dataset and show that they give the same estimates as each other and as existing implementations.
item.dc:creator: Tom Palmer, Nicolai Vitt, Eleanor Sanderson

item.title: Hybrid Federated Learning for Multimodal Fusion under Missing Modalities and Site Heterogeneity
item.description: arXiv:2611.03032v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal fusion is studied under hybrid federation, where data are partitioned across samples and feature blocks. The proposed two-dimensional federated smooth multiple-kernel large-margin learning method (2D-FedSMKL) integrates availability-corrected modality scores, group-kernel regularization, and smooth worst-site risk aggregation. For fixed maps and propensities, the objective is convex and smooth. Curvature bounds and exact synchronous block-gradient equivalence are established for binary and multiclass scores, giving a conditional accelerated rate. An oracle-propensity binary risk bound and a propensity-perturbation result are also derived. Simulations and two public activity-recognition benchmarks assess site heterogeneity and modality absence. Worst-site aggregation improves worst-site performance under heterogeneity, including reversed and size-balanced designs. On the benchmarks, validation selects the correction; the selected model is not significantly worse than the strongest reference at the worst site, and group-regularization benefits vary by dataset.
item.dc:creator: Xiaofei Wu, Rongmei Liang, Jian Qing Shi

item.title: Reducing SNAP Payment Errors at Lower Cost With AI: A Simulation Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.03213v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: New federal legislation will require states with high payment error rates in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) to pay a share of benefit costs, potentially costing some states over a billion dollars per year. These costs create substantial pressure to improve payment accuracy. One strategy to improve payment accuracy is preauthorization review, in which staff double-check applications and correct mistakes before benefits are issued. But limited staff capacity makes it important to target these reviews effectively. One leading targeting approach uses statistical risk models to prioritize cases likely to contain errors. Another novel approach uses AI to flag specific potential discrepancies for reviewers to check. For states under pressure to reduce error rates, it is unclear which approach-or combination of approaches-would reduce payment error rates most effectively. We compare these strategies through simulations using public SNAP quality control data. Under our main assumptions, risk-based review alone costs about seven times as much as combining AI flags with risk scores. This cost advantage persists across a wide range of plausible assumptions. Our findings suggest that AI-assisted preauthorization review could be a key tool to help states avoid substantial cost-sharing obligations.
item.dc:creator: Alex Chohlas-Wood

item.title: Six-hourly Probabilistic Precipitation Forecasts Created From Hourly Probabilities
item.description: arXiv:2611.03326v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A lightweight neural network is described that produces six-hourly, spatially detailed probabilistic quantitative precipitation forecasts (PQPF) from a sequence of hourly spatially detailed probabilistic forecasts, for lead times from 6 to 72\,h. The hourly forecasts were generated by a ``zero-inflated'' Attention Residual U-Net that outputs the parameters of a probability distribution including a probability of no precipitation and a weighted mixture of two Gamma distributions at each grid point for each hourly forecast lead time. The six-hourly network passes the six consecutive hourly parameter sets, together with summary statistics of the spatial texture of the raw deterministic forecast, through a small recurrent (GRU) layer and a multi-layer perceptron, and maps them to a corresponding zero-inflated mixture of three Gamma distributions describing the six-hourly accumulated precipitation. Training uses sets of hourly probabilistic forecasts, drawn preferentially from wet and heavy-precipitation cases (importance sampling), and matched Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) six-hourly precipitation accumulations, subject to a quality threshold. The resulting six-hourly probabilistic forecasts are well calibrated and skillful, as demonstrated by reliability diagrams, performance diagrams and Brier Skill Scores evaluated over an out-of-sample period spanning day 12 through the end of every month of 2025. The Brier Skill Scores are consistently and significantly higher than those of a baseline that sums independent draws from the hourly distributions. Forecasts show realistic modulation of precipitation related to terrain variations
item.dc:creator: Thomas M Hamill

item.title: Methods for Assessing Distributional Assumptions in Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Tests
item.description: arXiv:2611.03333v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) studies is commonly based on bivariate generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) that assume normally distributed study-specific random effects. In practice, this distributional assumption is rarely examined, particularly in individual participant data meta-analysis (IPDMA), where empirical Bayes (EB) estimates exhibit heterogeneous precision across studies. Applying standard multivariate normality tests to such estimates can therefore lead to misleading inference. We propose a weighted extension of the Henze-Zirkler (HZ) test to assess bivariate normality of random effects, accounting for study-specific precision via inverse-variance weighting. To obtain valid finite-sample inference, we develop a parametric bootstrap calibration procedure. Extensive simulation studies showed that the classical HZ test applied to EB estimates can exhibit substantial Type I error inflation, whereas the proposed weighted procedures maintain nominal error rates while retaining power to detect departures from normality. The proposed method provides a practical, statistically principled diagnostic tool for assessing random-effects distributional assumptions in hierarchical models, with particular relevance to IPDMA of DTA studies. Although motivated by IPDMA, the proposed approach also extends to aggregate-data diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis based on study-level 2-by-2 tables.
item.dc:creator: Diribsa T. Bedada, Zelalem F. Negeri

item.title: Soccer: a quantitative analysis of team resilience and the miracle of Bern
item.description: arXiv:2203.06933v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Resilience is the ability to positively respond to adversity. It has been studied in psychology for several decades, with focus on how individuals overcome traumata or cope with setbacks and obstacles in their professional career. Research on resilience in the sport context is rather new. Activities are based on insights that in highly competitive environments, tiny effects tip the scales. A key question of measuring resilience in sports is what parameters to measure. Here a novel concept is proposed to measure the resilience of soccer teams. The relative frequency of matches is determined, where a soccer team, which is initially trailing by 2 goals, finally succeeds to win the match or at least to reach a draw. The analysis is applied to the last 59 seasons of the German premier soccer league Bundesliga. The empirical data are compared with a theoretical model derived from Poisson distributions. It is shown how leading teams in the premier soccer league differ from the average with respect to resilience, which provides further insights into the hidden secrets of top soccer teams.
item.dc:creator: Ralph St\"ommer

item.title: Anticipating Continued Global Fertility Decline via Neural Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2605.23858v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As fertility falls across much of the world, major projection systems disagree about whether decline will give way to recovery, reflecting different assumptions about post-transitional fertility. We ask instead what the historical record suggests, using NeuralTFR, a recurrent neural network that learns fertility dynamics solely from pooled histories of 230 countries and territories. In out-of-sample forecasts from three origins, it predicts fifteen years ahead as accurately as the United Nations' Bayesian model, and its prediction intervals score slightly better. Its forecasts reveal a simple nonlinear relationship, which a spline regression reproduces with similar accuracy: fertility tends to rise slightly from the lowest levels and decline from higher ones, with recent trends affecting the size of these changes more than their direction. By 2038, these dynamics leave very low fertility, below 1.5 births per woman, more widespread than the United Nations expects, without the extreme lows of the most pessimistic projections.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Ciganda, Facundo Morini, Francisco Piriz, Henrik-Alexander Schubert, Ugofilippo Basellini, Mikko Myrskyl\"a

item.title: Critique of "Use of roster charts in the investigation and prosecution of nurses ..." by John O' Quigley
item.description: arXiv:2606.29394v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The paper "Use of roster charts in the investigation and prosecution of nurses suspected of inflicting deliberate harm on patients" by Prof. John O'Quigley explores an interesting hypothesis concerning statistical information hidden in the part of the infamous Lucy Letby roster chart pertaining to the 37 other nurses. Unfortunately, we have to point out some serious errors in his statistical analyses. The data actually contains information which strongly disproves his main modelling assumption. We do, however, strongly agree with him that from a forensic statistical point of view, the roster chart is fake evidence which should not have been shown to jurors.
item.dc:creator: Richard D. Gill

item.title: Temporal Seam Score for Assessing Continuity at Known Transitions in Time Series
item.description: arXiv:2609.15132v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long environmental records increasingly combine observations from successive observing or processing systems. Transitions between these systems create temporal seams that may reflect imperfect harmonization or changes in the observed process. We introduce the Temporal Seam Score (S-score, or S), a signed, robust measure for assessing continuity at a known transition time. The complete time series is fitted with a seam-blind model accounting for trend, seasonality, and optional covariates. The residual contrast between symmetric windows around the transition is compared with matched reference contrasts calculated within the contributing segments. The S-score is the standardized departure of the seam contrast from this reference. An S-score near zero indicates that the seam is consistent with ordinary temporal variability. Its sign indicates the direction of the discontinuity, while its magnitude (|S|) indicates how exceptional the discontinuity is. Simulation showed that |S| reflects the imposed discontinuity relative to residual variability: a 20% shift produced a median |S| of 2.58 at a residual coefficient of variation of 0.10, compared with 0.84 at 0.50. In a MODIS-to-Sentinel-3 vegetation record, 121 of 500 sites yielded finite S-scores, of which 90 met all reliability criteria. Among these reliable sites, median S was +0.217 and median |S| was 0.627, indicating little systematic directional displacement and a median seam departure below one reference spread. The S-score provides a general and auditable diagnostic for evaluating temporal continuity across generations of sensors, algorithms, and observing systems without requiring temporal overlap, thereby supporting harmonization quality assurance and more reliable attribution analyses based on long-term environmental records.
item.dc:creator: Hongxiao Jin

item.title: Are New Parties Shut Out of the UK House of Commons?
item.description: arXiv:2610.28866v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In recent years it has been claimed that new political parties are shut out of the UK House of Commons because they are rarely elected. At the same time, general political understanding seems to be that the House of Commons is currently further away from a pure two-party distribution of seats than at any time in the past century, perhaps longer. Although this might seem like a paradox it is possible for both of these things to have credence. We present an analysis that shows that the number of new political parties elected to the House of Commons has been slowly declining over the last century. We illustrate this both by regression and Good-Turing analyses. We also analyse the lifetime and persistence of political parties as well as present metrics that indicate the recent increased political diversity and identify the nadir of diversity in the mid-1960s and early 1970s.
item.dc:creator: Guy P. Nason

item.title: Causal DAG-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Physical Activity Maintenance: Using Prior Data to Inform Future Deployment
item.description: arXiv:2610.36019v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Digital health interventions can provide scalable, personalized support for physical activity (PA), yet sustaining PA over the long-term remains difficult. Because affective experiences with PA are important for activity sustainment, we developed an online reinforcement learning (RL) system for the forthcoming ADAPT factorial trial that personalizes twice-daily activity suggestions aimed at improving affective associations with PA. This setting poses several challenges: participant-specific data are scarce relative to the candidate state space, important states and rewards are partially observed, interventions are frequent while the primary outcome is measured weekly, and activity suggestions can both improve PA-related experiences and increase intervention burden. We address these challenges using an expert-specified causal directed acyclic graph as an integrated RL design tool, guiding state construction, estimation of partially observed states, delayed credit assignment, and representation of beneficial and adverse intervention pathways. We further construct a longitudinal simulator calibrated from a prior micro-randomized trial to compare candidate RL designs under realistic state evolution, missingness, and participant heterogeneity before deployment. Together, this work illustrates how causal domain knowledge and prior trial data can make long-horizon, participant-specific RL more practical for digital health interventions targeting sustained behavior change.
item.dc:creator: Xueqing Liu, Young Hyun Cho, Bhanu Teja Gullapalli, Predrag Klasnja, Susan Murphy

item.title: Stage-wise semiparametric analysis of multivariate event times under informative censoring via vine copula
item.description: arXiv:2502.20608v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The analysis of times to multiple nonterminal events arises in many lifetime data settings, where the nonterminal event times are subject to informative censoring by a terminal event, posing substantial challenges. We propose a likelihood-based regression framework that models dependence among multiple nonterminal and terminal event times using a vine copula. This framework allows pairwise associations between nonterminal and terminal events, as well as among nonterminal events, to vary across event types, while enabling valid regression inference for the marginal distributions of individual event times. To facilitate computation, we develop a stage-wise pseudo-likelihood estimation procedure and establish its large-sample properties. We demonstrate satisfactory finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators and associated variance estimators through simulation studies. We also illustrate the proposed methodology using data from a crowdfunding platform to examine the relationship between different types of creator-backer interactions and a creator's lifetime on the platform.
item.dc:creator: Xinyuan Chen, Yiwei Li, Qian M. Zhou

item.title: Statistical Machine Learning for Astronomy -- A Textbook
item.description: arXiv:2506.12230v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This textbook gives a systematic treatment of statistical machine learning for astronomical research, based on Bayesian inference. It shows how modern data analysis techniques connect to classical statistical methods and follow from familiar statistical principles. The Bayesian perspective, used throughout, gives priority to uncertainty quantification and statistical rigor, which scientific inference in astronomy needs. The textbook progresses from probability theory and Bayesian inference through supervised learning, including linear regression with measurement uncertainties, logistic regression and classification. Unsupervised learning topics cover Principal Component Analysis and clustering methods. We then introduce sampling and Markov Chain Monte Carlo, followed by Gaussian Processes as probabilistic nonparametric methods and neural networks in the broader statistical context. Our theory-focused approach derives each method from first principles with complete mathematical development and then shows its astronomical applications. We put statistical insight first and explain why algorithms work, when they are appropriate, and how they connect to broader statistical principles. From a solid grounding in classical methods and their theory, the treatment leads to modern techniques such as neural networks. With this grounding, readers can apply the methods to astronomical research with proper attention to assumptions, limits and uncertainty propagation, as large astronomical surveys require. The 22 companion tutorials apply the methods to astronomical data in Jupyter notebooks.
item.dc:creator: Yuan-Sen Ting

item.title: AQBuc: Air Pollution Forecasting in Bucharest
item.description: arXiv:2511.00532v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In recent years, air pollution, especially the particulate matter $2.5\,\mu\text{m}$ (PM2.5), has become a growing concern mainly in urban areas. Exposure to air pollution is linked to the development of numerous health conditions, such as the aggravation of respiratory diseases, cardiovascular disorders, impaired lung function, and even cancer or early death. Forecasting future levels of PM2.5 has become increasingly important, as it can provide early warnings and help prevent diseases. We propose AQBuc, a dataset for predicting PM2.5 pollution in Bucharest, Romania, introducing an understudied location, as most work in this field has focused on Asian cities. Our dataset allows us to benchmark models for predicting future levels of PM2.5 across various time horizons. We evaluate a broad range of methods, including machine learning models, such as linear regression and ensemble-based methods, deep learning models based on recurrent networks and transformers, and large language models (LLMs). Specialized time-series models handle temporal data better, especially on longer horizons, while tree ensembles are more cost-effective for short horizons. Meanwhile, LLMs struggle to capture continuous sensor dynamics without specialized architectural changes.
item.dc:creator: Drago\c{s}-Andrei \c{S}erban, R\u{a}zvan-Alexandru Sm\u{a}du, Dumitru-Clementin Cercel

item.title: Differential Dynamic Causal Nets: Model Construction, Identification and Group Comparisons
item.description: arXiv:2601.21478v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pathophysiological modelling of brain systems from microscale to macroscale remains difficult in group comparisons partly because of the infeasibility of modelling the interactions of thousands of neurons at the scales involved. Here, to address the challenge, we present a novel approach to construct differential causal networks directly from grouped electroencephalogram (EEG) data. In the proposed modular network, each node represents a locally averaged regional neural system via a canonical Jansen-Rit model while directed edges stand for node-wise input-output connections. The network is hierarchically structured in the sense that node and edge parameters are random, varying in subjects, but follow a mixed-effects model. We show that unlike the classical Jansen-Rit models, the proposed node models are locally structurally identifiable. An evolutionary optimisation algorithm for parameter inference in the proposed method is developed using a loss function derived from Chen-Fliess expansions of stochastic differential equations. The method is demonstrated by fitting the proposed modular network to grouped epileptic EEG data in both sensor- and source- levels. We identify significant changes in the parameters that characterise dynamic networks within and between brain regions. We reveal network disruptions, due to imbalance of excitatory-inhibitory interneurons and other altered epileptic brain connectivities, before and during seizure periods, and contrast them between case and control groups. The performance of the proposed method is also evaluated on synthetic data.
item.dc:creator: Kang You, Gary Green, Jian Zhang

item.title: Selecting Hyperparameters for Tree-Boosting
item.description: arXiv:2602.05786v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tree-boosting is a widely used machine learning technique for tabular data. However, its out-of-sample accuracy is critically dependent on multiple hyperparameters. In this article, we empirically compare several popular methods for hyperparameter optimization for tree-boosting including random grid search, the tree-structured Parzen estimator (TPE), Gaussian-process-based Bayesian optimization (GP-BO), Hyperband, the sequential model-based algorithm configuration (SMAC) method, and deterministic full grid search using $59$ regression and binary classification data sets. We find that the SMAC method clearly outperforms all the other considered methods on average, and it gives stable performance across a diverse collection of tabular data sets under a fixed tuning budget, which is relevant for users who cannot afford extensive manual trial-and-error tuning. We further observe that (i) a relatively large number of trials larger than $100$ is typically required for accurate tuning, (ii) using default values for hyperparameters or a full search over a small grid often yields very inaccurate models, (iii) all considered hyperparameters can have a material effect on the accuracy of tree-boosting, i.e., there is no small set of hyperparameters that is more important than others, and (iv) choosing the number of boosting iterations using early stopping yields more accurate results compared to including it in the search space for regression tasks.
item.dc:creator: Floris Jan Koster, Fabio Sigrist

item.title: Zero Variance Portfolio
item.description: arXiv:2602.19462v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When the number of assets is larger than the sample size, the minimum variance portfolio interpolates the training data, delivering pathological zero in-sample variance. We show that if the weights of the zero variance portfolio are learned by a novel ``Ridgelet'' estimator, in a new test data this portfolio enjoys out-of-sample generalizability. It exhibits the double descent phenomenon and can achieve optimal risk in the overparametrized regime when the number of assets dominates the sample size. In contrast, a ``Ridgeless'' estimator which invokes the pseudoinverse fails in-sample interpolation and diverges away from out-of-sample optimality. Extensive simulations and empirical studies demonstrate that the Ridgelet method performs competitively in high-dimensional portfolio optimization.
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Chang, Yi Ding, Zhentao Shi, Bo Zhang

item.title: Adapting Altman's bankruptcy prediction model to the compositional data methodology
item.description: arXiv:2603.24215v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Using standard financial ratios as variables in statistical analyses has been related to several serious problems, such as extreme outliers, asymmetry, non-normality, and nonlinearity. The compositional-data methodology has been successfully applied to solve these problems and has always yielded substantially different results when compared to standard financial ratios. An under-researched area is the use of financial log-ratios computed with the compositional-data methodology to predict bankruptcy or the related terms of business default, insolvency or failure. Another under-researched area is the use of machine learning methods in combination with compositional log-ratios. The present article adapts the classical Altman bankruptcy prediction model and some of its extensions to the compositional methodology with pairwise log-ratios and three common statistical and machine learning tools: logistic regression models, k-nearest neighbours, and random forests, and compares the results with standard financial ratios. Data from the sector in the Spanish economy with the largest number of bankrupt firms according to the first two digits of the NACE code (46XX "wholesale trade, except of motor vehicles and motorcycles") were obtained from the Iberian Balance sheet Analysis System. The sample size (31,131 firms, of which 97 were bankrupt) was divided into a training and a validation dataset. The training dataset was downsampled to one healthy firm to each bankrupt firm. No outliers were removed. Focusing on predictive performance, the results show that compositional methods are better than standard ratios in terms of sensitivity (recall), with mixed results regarding specificity, compositional random forests and compositional logistic regression behaving the best.
item.dc:creator: Fatemeh Keivani (Universitat de Girona), Germ\`a Coenders (Universitat de Girona), Ge\`orgia Escaram\'is (Universitat de Girona, CEEISCAT. Department of Health. Government of Catalonia)

item.title: Revisiting Certified Defense with Differential Privacy on Vision Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2609.31310v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Certified defenses that incorporate differential privacy have proven effective on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), furnishing rigorous robustness guarantees against norm-bounded adversaries. However, the certified robustness behavior of Pixel Differential Privacy (PixelDP) remains largely unexplored with the self-attention architecture now dominating the deep-learning landscape. Given that the Transformer has a profound impact on our daily applications from the digital world to the physical world, it is crucial to study certified robustness through differential-privacy-style stability. To fill this research gap, we revisit this construction in Vision Transformers and identify a failure mode that is largely hidden in the convolutional setting. When noise is injected after the patch embedding, the Laplace mechanism with the inherited grouped $\ell_1$ sensitivity bound collapses to chance-level accuracy across noise scales, whereas the Gaussian mechanism remains trainable. This contrast isolates the source of failure: not the injected noise itself, but the geometry of the sensitivity constraint. We show that the attenuation induced by the inherited $\Delta_{1,1}$ projection increases with layer width and kernel size according to a random-matrix scale $C/(\sqrt{M}+\sqrt{N})$. Replacing the $\ell_1$-type constraint with a spectral-norm constraint eliminates the collapse across datasets and architectures, but creates a fundamental obstacle: the repaired models no longer satisfy the sensitivity condition required by the standard Laplace certificate. We resolve this mismatch by deriving a dimension-free $(\varepsilon,\ \delta)$-privacy guarantee for the Laplace mechanism under $\ell_2$ sensitivity through concentration of the privacy loss.
item.dc:creator: Jun Yan, Weiquan Huang, Qixian Zhang, Yan Bai, Shutai Zhang

item.title: Reliability Engineering for AI Systems: Challenges, Methods, and Directions
item.description: arXiv:2609.35316v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI reliability concerns whether an AI system performs its intended function dependably over a stated period and under stated operating conditions, with stated evidence. As these systems become more autonomous, that function includes more than a correct output. Retrieval, memory, tool use, permissions, human oversight, and interactions among systems must operate consistently and safely, and, for generative systems, so must the reasoning process that produces the output. Average benchmark accuracy measures capability; it does not quantify this broader reliability claim. This paper adapts established reliability engineering methods, from failure definitions and operational envelopes to FMEA, accelerated testing, field monitoring, and reliability growth, to AI systems. A four-level diagnostic framework classifies failures as component, operational-loop, agentic-conduct, or network and governance failures. Test, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV), sequential monitoring, and FRACAS create and refresh evidence. SMART provides statistical guidance for measurement, analysis, assessment, and test planning; the NIST AI Risk Management Framework provides organizational guidance for governance, evaluation, monitoring, and mitigation. Three cases illustrate the program: adversarial testing of a convolutional neural network, perception-error propagation, and autonomous-vehicle disengagements. Established reliability engineering provides a usable foundation; new measurements and safety guardrails are still needed as these systems are self-evolving.
item.dc:creator: Rong Pan, Yili Hong, Min Xie

item.title: Global Parameter Identification and Uncertainty Quantification of reduced-order ADM1 using Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Bayesian Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.19098v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) models can be challenging to calibrate against real data due to limited practical identifiability, data scarcity, and model complexity. Weighted least squares objective functions and gradient-based solvers using finite differences are often used in literature, but result in suboptimal parameter estimates and large uncertainty bands. This paper identifies the parameters of a reduced-order ADM1 by comparing the frameworks of maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and Bayesian inference (BI), and quantifies uncertainties of parameters and outputs. Multirate experimental data are taken from a lab-scale AD reactor fed with agricultural substrates and operated at organic loading rates of 3$\,$g VS $\mathrm{m^{-3}d^{-1}}$. Global optima are found via global and gradient-based local search algorithms using forward sensitivities. Enhanced scatter search provides the best global search results. These are refined by the Gauss-Newton algorithm as the best local search, which delivers $R^2$ values of 0.95 for acetic acid and 0.77 for biogas production. BI yields substantially narrower uncertainty bands than MLE and avoids the need for a global search by incorporating prior knowledge about parameter distributions. The search space is captured efficiently by log10 scaling of parameters. Algorithmic details on its implications are provided. Despite a high-resolution lab-scale dataset, the ADM1-specific inhibition parameter $K_\mathrm{I,nh3}$ is practically not identifiable with MLE, and shows a low output sensitivity, whereas a parameter for the effective ion concentration shows superb practical identifiabilty at high confidence with both MLE and BI. The present work lays a scalable base for calibration of nonlinear AD models by providing reliable simulations. It thus advances model-based monitoring and control applications of multirate processes such as agricultural AD plants.
item.dc:creator: Simon Hellmann, Leander Lerch, Terrance Wilms, Moritz Reumsch\"ussel, Alberto Meola, F\'elix Delory, Steffi Knorn, Stefan Streif, S\"oren Weinrich
